docs.title: Frappe Microservice Framework
docs.text:
Build secure, independently deployable microservices on top of Frappe and ERPNext — without changing how you write Frappe code.

Each service owns its own database while a Central Site stays the single source of truth for authentication. Your DocTypes, controllers and hooks work as they always have; the framework handles isolation, auth, tenancy and container startup.

The goal is gradual decomposition: peel Sales, HR or Inventory out of an ERPNext monolith one module at a time, rather than attempting a big-bang rewrite.

docs.title: What it gives you
docs.text:
• Auto-CRUD — app.register_resource("Sales Order") exposes a DocType as a documented REST resource with no handler code.
  • Secure by default — every secure_route authenticates against the Central Site and injects the resolved user. OAuth2 Bearer tokens, sid cookies and an internal service token are all supported.
  • Bounded context — a service owns its schema and database, so it can be deployed and scaled on its own.
  • Optional multi-tenancy — automatic tenant_id scoping on every read and write, or turn it off entirely and run against a stock site.
  • Frappe-native — DocType controllers and lifecycle hooks, with no changes to Frappe core.
  • Container-first — the base image ships the entrypoint, syncs DocType schema at startup, and logs to stderr. Liveness and readiness probes are built in.
  • Background jobs — an embedded RQ worker, with Frappe context restored.
  • Observability — OpenTelemetry tracing and container-safe logging.

docs.text: Getting Started Install, first service, container deployment Configuration Every environment variable and kwarg Tenancy Single- vs multi-tenant, and the Central Site contract Core Features CRUD, controllers, hooks, jobs, Swagger, probes Security Policy modes, authentication, SQL safety Architecture Bounded context, isolation, decomposition Observability Tracing and logging CI/CD Pipeline, image tags, framework versions Developer Guide Tests, linting, where to make changes Dependency Slimming How the image stays small

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Frappe v16 and Python 3.10+.

docs.title: The problem this solves
docs.text:
A Frappe app expects to be one of several apps installed on one site, sharing one database, one Redis, and one hooks registry. A microservice needs the opposite: its own database, its own schema, and no visibility into other services' apps.

The framework reconciles the two by patching Frappe's app- and module-resolution at startup so a service sees only itself plus the framework apps it declares — without forking Frappe or changing how you write DocTypes and controllers.

docs.title: Package structure
docs.text:
frappe_microservice/
├── __init__.py        # public API surface
├── core.py            # re-export shim (backward compatibility)
├── app.py             # MicroserviceApp + create_microservice()
├── auth.py            # AuthMixin — OAuth2 / SID / internal-token validation
├── background.py      # BackgroundTaskMixin — embedded RQ worker
├── cache.py           # Redis key namespacing for a shared cache
├── central.py         # CentralSiteClient (app.central)
├── cli.py             # `frappe-ms` CLI
├── controller.py      # DocumentController + registry
├── entrypoint.py      # container entrypoint (SERVICE_PATH / SERVICE_APP)
├── hooks.py           # DocumentHooks lifecycle system
├── isolation.py       # IsolationMixin — app/module/hook filtering
├── naming.py          # tenant-scoped docnames, resolve-or-create
├── policy.py          # resolve_mode / resolve_bool flag parsing
├── presentation.py    # Link-value label presentation
├── presync.py         # startup DocType schema + fixture sync
├── resources.py       # ResourceMixin — register_resource() auto-CRUD
├── site_config.py     # site_config.json generation
├── tenant.py          # TenantAwareDB, tenant resolution
└── utils.py

Everything public is importable from both frappe_microservice and frappe_microservice.core; the latter is a compatibility shim.

graph TD
    app[app.py<br/>MicroserviceApp] --> isolation[isolation.py]
    app --> auth[auth.py]
    app --> resources[resources.py]
    app --> background[background.py]
    app --> tenant[tenant.py]
    app --> central[central.py]
    app --> siteconfig[site_config.py]
    tenant --> hooks[hooks.py]
    tenant --> naming[naming.py]
    resources --> presentation[presentation.py]
    isolation --> presync[presync.py]
    isolation --> cache[cache.py]
    app --> policy[policy.py]
Module Owns app.py MicroserviceApp (composed from the mixins), create_microservice(), secure_route, middleware auth.py OAuth2 Bearer, Frappe sid session, and X-Internal-Token validation background.py Embedded RQ worker thread and enqueue_task cache.py Prefixes cache keys so services can share one Redis central.py CentralSiteClient — service→Central Site calls controller.py Frappe-style DocumentController classes and discovery hooks.py DocumentHooks — register/run lifecycle hooks per DocType isolation.py Patches frappe.get_installed_apps, module maps and hook resolution naming.py Tenant-scoped docnames; resolve_or_create for master doctypes policy.py Shared off/warn/enforce and boolean flag parsing presentation.py Presents renamed-master Link values as their labels presync.py Startup DocType schema sync and fixture import resources.py register_resource() auto-CRUD endpoints site_config.py Generates site_config.json from the environment tenant.py TenantAwareDB, tenant resolution, tenant_id stamping

docs.title: Bounded context
docs.text:
Each service owns its data. The Central Site remains the authority for authentication and global user state; the service database holds only the DocTypes in that service's bounded context.

services:
  orders-service:
    image: ghcr.io/vyogotech/erpnext-microservices-lib:latest
    environment:
      DB_HOST: orders-db
      CENTRAL_SITE_URL: http://central-site:8000
    depends_on: [orders-db]

  orders-db:
    image: mariadb:10.6
    environment:
      MYSQL_DATABASE: orders_db
      MYSQL_USER: orders_user
      MYSQL_PASSWORD: orders_pass

docs.title: App and module isolation
docs.text:
A service container may have frappe and erpnext installed but must not load another service's app hooks. IsolationMixin patches Frappe so that:

  • frappe.get_installed_apps() returns only the allowed set (the framework apps declared via load_framework_hooks, plus this service's own app).
  • Module maps resolve only to modules the container can actually import.
  • Hook resolution skips paths belonging to non-allowed apps, rather than raising ModuleNotFoundError when the Central Site's apps appear in a shared cache.

A broken import inside an allowed app still propagates — that is a real bug and is deliberately not swallowed as a skipped hook.

docs.title: Shared Redis cache
docs.text: Frappe prefixes cache keys with the database name. Services sharing a database name would therefore collide on keys like app_hooks or doctype_meta:<doctype>. The framework patches RedisWrapper.make_key at startup to add the service name to every non-shared key, so several services and the Central Site can share one Redis instance safely. Keys explicitly requested with shared=True bypass namespacing and reach the global namespace.

docs.title: Startup schema sync
docs.text:
At container startup entrypoint.main() runs presync_service_doctypes() once, before Gunicorn forks workers; in dev (app.run()) it syncs lazily on the first request. DOCTYPE_SYNC_MODE selects the behaviour — see Schema sync.

Concurrent replicas are safe: the sync body takes a database advisory lock (MariaDB GET_LOCK, Postgres pg_advisory_lock), and a replica that cannot acquire it within 120s skips the sync rather than crashing. For operators who prefer an explicit migration step, frappe-ms migrate runs the same sync and suits a Kubernetes Job.

docs.title: Tenancy
docs.text:
The framework supports a single site, multi-tenant model where rows carry a tenant_id, and an equally first-class single-tenant mode where they do not. See Tenancy for the modes, the Central Site contract and how to choose.

In multi-tenant mode, app.tenant_db ensures:

  1. Filtering — reads (get_all, count, exists, get_value) carry a tenant_id filter.
  2. Verification — get_doc confirms the document belongs to the current tenant before returning it.
  3. Stamping — insert_doc sets tenant_id from the request context.

docs.title: Request flow
docs.text:
graph LR
    User[End user] --> MS[Microservice]
    MS --> Auth[Central Site auth]
    MS --> DB[(Service DB)]
    DB -- "tenant_id scoping" --> Data[Tenant data]
  1. The user authenticates against the Central Site.
  2. The microservice receives the request with a sid cookie or Bearer token.
  3. secure_route validates the session against the Central Site.
  4. In multi-tenant mode the user's tenant_id is resolved into flask.g.
  5. Database operations through app.tenant_db are scoped accordingly.

docs.title: Decomposing an ERPNext monolith
docs.text:
The framework exists to make decomposition incremental rather than a big-bang migration:

  1. Identify a module — Orders, Inventory, HR.
  2. Define its bounded context — move the relevant DocTypes to a service database.
  3. Build the service — expose APIs and business logic with this framework.
  4. Keep auth unified — the Central Site stays the single point of entry.
  5. Scale independently — give order processing more replicas than the rest.

Each extraction is reversible and independently deployable, which is what keeps the risk bounded.

docs.title: CI/CD & Release
docs.text:
The pipeline lives in .github/workflows/ci.yml and runs four jobs in a strict chain. Each gates the next, so an image is only published if both the unit and integration suites passed.

test ──► integration-test ──► build ──► verify-image

Triggers: pushes to main, release, develop, version-*; tags v*; pull requests against those branches; and manual dispatch.

docs.title: test
docs.text:
Python 3.10. Installs the package with pip install -e ".[dev]", then:

flake8 frappe_microservice/
PYTHONPATH=. pytest -m "not integration" --alluredir=allure-results tests/
PYTHONPATH=. behave -f allure_behave.formatter:AllureFormatter -o allure-results features/

Allure results are uploaded as an artifact (1-day retention, non-blocking).

docs.title: integration-test
docs.text:
Brings up docker-compose.integration.yml — the public docker.io/vyogo/erpnext:sne-version-16 single-node image, with the repository bind-mounted at /mnt/lib and MULTI_TENANT=0.

It waits up to 400s for the site to answer SELECT 1, bootstraps ERPNext test data if no Company exists, installs the library into the bench virtualenv, and runs tests/integration/ with branch coverage.

This job uses no registry credentials, deliberately. GITHUB_TOKEN is restricted on pull requests from forks, so requiring a login would make the integration suite unrunnable for outside contributors. That is why the base image is public on Docker Hub rather than private on GHCR.

docs.title: build
docs.text:
Builds with docker/setup-buildx-action + docker/build-push-action. It builds twice:

  1. Verification build (push: false, load: true) — then runs scripts/check_pruned_deps.py inside the image. That script walk-imports every Frappe and ERPNext module to prove the dependency pruning did not remove something a controller reaches transitively. It also reports image size.
  2. Publish build (push: true) — largely served from the first build's buildx cache.

Platform is linux/amd64 only. arm64 via QEMU cost roughly 15 minutes per build; the intended path when it is needed is a native runner per architecture pushing :tag-amd64 / :tag-arm64, stitched with docker buildx imagetools create.

docs.title: verify-image
docs.text:
Runs only on manual dispatch, or on a push to main or release. Pulls the image that was just published — by its SHA tag, not a rebuild — and re-runs tests/integration/ inside it via scripts/run_service_image_integration.sh. Expected: 12 passed, 9 skipped.

The 9 skips are all of test_tenant_id_stamping.py; a service image does not ship a tenancy provider app.

docs.title: Image tags
docs.text:
The image name is derived from the repository: ghcr.io/vyogotech/erpnext-microservices-lib.

Tags come from docker/metadata-action:

Event Tags produced push main latest, sha-<short>, sha-<full> push develop / version-* branch name, sha-<short>, sha-<full> push release sha-<short>, sha-<full> only push tag v* the tag name (e.g. v1.5.0), sha-<short>, sha-<full> pull request pr-<number> — and it is pushed

Two things worth internalising:

  • latest only ever means main. A v* tag push does not move latest.
  • Every non-PR build gets both SHA tags. These are the immutable references — use sha-<full> for reproducible deploys, never latest.

Fork pull requests cannot push

The build job pushes on pull requests, but GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only for packages on fork PRs, so that step fails for outside contributors — the same constraint integration-test is designed around.

docs.title: Framework versions
docs.text:
The Containerfile takes FRAPPE_VERSION and ERPNEXT_VERSION build arguments, pinned by default to immutable tags:

FRAPPE_VERSION=v16.28.0
ERPNEXT_VERSION=v16.29.0

Branches override them:

Branch / event FRAPPE_VERSION ERPNEXT_VERSION develop, or a PR based on it develop develop version-15*, or a PR based on it version-15 version-15 everything else (main, release, version-16, tags, dispatch) v16.28.0 v16.29.0

There is no version-16 special case — that branch builds against the pinned v16 tags, which is what "version-16" means in practice.

The library requires Frappe v16

frappe_microservice.app imports frappe.utils.local, which does not exist in Frappe v15. A version-15 build fails at import. That override exists for the maintenance branch, not for main.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: .github/workflows/docs.yml runs on pushes to main: installs mkdocs-material and publishes to gh-pages with mkdocs gh-deploy --force.

docs.title: Running the pipeline locally
docs.text:
act runs jobs on your machine (requires Docker or Podman):

act -j test --container-architecture linux/arm64

.actrc maps ubuntu-latest to catthehacker/ubuntu:act-latest. The integration-test job needs a container runtime and pulls a ~1.5 GB image, so it is slow locally — the scripts in Development are the better path.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Every option is an environment variable; many also have a create_microservice(...) keyword argument. The keyword argument wins over the environment variable, which wins over the default.

docs.title: How values resolve
docs.text:
Two helpers in frappe_microservice/policy.py parse configuration, and their empty-value handling is deliberate:

Boolean flags (resolve_bool) accept 1, true, yes, on (case-insensitive). An unset or empty variable falls back to the default — so a Kubernetes env: entry with no value, or a missing ConfigMap key, cannot silently flip a security flag that defaults on. Any other non-empty string is read as false: MULTI_TENANT=disabled means off, not the default.

Tri-state modes (resolve_mode) accept off, warn, enforce. Unset falls back to the default silently; an unknown or empty value falls back with a logged warning rather than failing to boot.

docs.title: Tenancy
docs.text: Variable Kwarg Values Default Purpose MULTI_TENANT multi_tenant 1/true/yes/on on Master switch for tenant isolation. See Tenancy

docs.title: Security policy modes
docs.text:
See Security for what each mode does and how to roll them out.

Variable Kwarg Values Default 2.0 default PERMISSION_MODE permission_mode off\|warn\|enforce warn enforce CSRF_MODE csrf_mode off\|warn\|enforce warn enforce TENANT_STRICT tenant_strict off\|warn\|enforce warn enforce MASK_PERMISSION_ERRORS mask_permission_errors 1/true/yes/on off on INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN — secret unset (path disabled) — INTERNAL_SERVICE_USER — username Administrator — ALLOW_CORS — origin string * and a warning explicit

ALLOW_CORS is written into site_config.json. An explicitly empty value is honoured as-is (effectively disabling CORS) rather than falling back to *.

docs.title: Site & database
docs.text:
Variable Kwarg Default Purpose FRAPPE_SITE frappe_site site1.local Frappe site name FRAPPE_SITES_PATH sites_path /app/sites Sites directory DB_HOST db_host unset Service database host DB_PORT — 3306 Port; ignored if DB_HOST_PORT is set DB_HOST_PORT — unset Kubernetes-style port; takes precedence DB_NAME — empty Database name DB_USER — falls back to DB_NAME, then frappe Database user DB_PASSWORD — changeme Database password ENCRYPTION_KEY — unset Frappe encryption_key; overridden by /secrets/encryption_key.txt when present REDIS_HOST — localhost Base Redis host REDIS_PORT — 6379 Redis port REDIS_CACHE_HOST — REDIS_HOST Overrides the cache host only REDIS_QUEUE_HOST — REDIS_HOST Overrides the queue host only REDIS_NAMESPACE — unset (key omitted) Frappe redis_namespace

Set FRAPPE_SITE explicitly

Left unset, the application initialises site site1.local while site_config.json is written under dev.localhost. The two only agree when you set FRAPPE_SITE. Always set it in a container.

docs.title: Central Site
docs.text:
Variable Default Purpose CENTRAL_SITE_URL http://central-site:8000 Base URL of the Central Site CENTRAL_SITE_API_KEY unset API key (token auth) CENTRAL_SITE_API_SECRET unset API secret (token auth) CENTRAL_SITE_USER unset Username (password auth) CENTRAL_SITE_PASSWORD unset Password (password auth) CENTRAL_SITE_TIMEOUT 10 Currently read but not applied to the client

Use either the key/secret pair or the user/password pair.

docs.title: Service discovery & container
docs.text: Variable Default Purpose SERVICE_PATH /app/service Service source root SERVICE_APP server:app WSGI target as module:attr SERVICE_NAME empty Name used for the doctypes path, advisory lock and Redis namespace PORT 8000 Gunicorn bind port (read by the entrypoint, not by MicroserviceApp) GUNICORN_WORKERS 4 Worker processes GUNICORN_TIMEOUT 120 Worker timeout, seconds

docs.title: Schema sync
docs.text:
At startup the entrypoint runs the DocType sync once, before Gunicorn forks workers; in dev (app.run()) it syncs lazily on the first request.

Variable Values Default Purpose DOCTYPE_SYNC_MODE migrate\|create migrate Schema sync behaviour FIXTURE_SYNC_MODE strict\|soft strict Whether a failed fixture aborts startup DOCTYPES_PATH path derived from SERVICE_PATH / SERVICE_NAME DocType JSON directory SERVICE_POST_PRESYNC module.attr unset Callable run after sync, inside the advisory lock
  • migrate (default) — create-if-missing and update-if-changed. Editing a DocType JSON and restarting updates both tabDocType metadata and the SQL table. It is additive only: columns are never dropped.
  • create — create-only, for operators who must not run DDL at startup.

FIXTURE_SYNC_MODE=strict is the default on purpose: a fixture is service-owned schema, so a failed import means the service is running against a schema it does not have. soft downgrades that to an error log and is intended for recovery.

Concurrent replicas are safe — the sync takes a database advisory lock, and a replica that cannot acquire it within 120s skips rather than crashing. For an explicit migration step, frappe-ms migrate runs the same sync and suits a Kubernetes Job.

docs.title: Background jobs
docs.text: Variable Values Default Purpose ENABLE_RQ 1/true/yes/on off Enable RQ and start the embedded worker REDIS_URL URL redis://localhost:6379 Redis for the queue — separate from REDIS_HOST WORKER_MODE exactly 1 unset Set up the queue but do not start the thread; run frappe-ms worker instead RQ_DEFAULT_JOB_TIMEOUT seconds -1 (none) Default job timeout

docs.title: Logging & observability
docs.text:
Variable Default Purpose LOG_LEVEL INFO Library log level; an unrecognised name falls back to INFO OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT unset (tracing off) OTLP collector endpoint FRAPPE_STREAM_LOGGING 1 Stream Frappe logs to stderr instead of files DEBUG unset Include exception detail in 500 bodies. Must be exactly 1

The library forces FRAPPE_STREAM_LOGGING=1 at import. Frappe's file handlers resolve paths relative to the process working directory — a bench-era assumption that crashes with FileNotFoundError: .../logs/database.log under a container WORKDIR or a read-only root filesystem. To opt back into file logs, set FRAPPE_STREAM_LOGGING="" before importing the library.

Under readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, the sites directory must stay writable — site_config.json is written there. Mount an emptyDir for it.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
A few options do not follow the general rules. These are accurate as of this version:

  • WORKER_MODE and DEBUG require exactly the string 1. Unlike the boolean flags, true / yes / on silently do nothing.
  • RQ_DEFAULT_JOB_TIMEOUT="" and CENTRAL_SITE_TIMEOUT="" raise ValueError. The database and Redis port helpers guard against empty values; these two do not. Leave them unset rather than empty.
  • CENTRAL_SITE_TIMEOUT has no effect — it is read but never applied to the client.
  • LOAD_FRAMEWORK_HOOKS only affects the presync path, not MicroserviceApp, and the two default differently ([] versus ["frappe", "erpnext"]). Prefer the load_framework_hooks kwarg, which accepts a list of app names or one of "full", "frappe-only", "none".

docs.title: Constructor-only options
docs.text:
These have no environment variable:

Kwarg Default Purpose name (positional) required Flask app name, RQ queue name, Redis namespace, OTel service name port 8000 Dev-server port for run() tenant_field tenant_id Tenant column name get_tenant_id_func None Custom tenant resolver doctypes_path None DocType JSON directory fixtures_path $SERVICE_PATH/fixtures if present Fixture directory controllers_path $SERVICE_PATH/controllers if present Controller discovery root load_framework_hooks ["frappe", "erpnext"] Framework apps whose hooks may load

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A starting point for a container deployment — see .env.example for the annotated version:

FRAPPE_SITE=dev.localhost
FRAPPE_SITES_PATH=/app/sites
DB_HOST=orders-db
DB_NAME=orders_db
REDIS_HOST=redis

CENTRAL_SITE_URL=http://central-site:8000
CENTRAL_SITE_API_KEY=...
CENTRAL_SITE_API_SECRET=...

MULTI_TENANT=1
TENANT_STRICT=warn
PERMISSION_MODE=warn
CSRF_MODE=warn
ALLOW_CORS=https://app.example.com

SERVICE_PATH=/app/service
SERVICE_APP=server:app
DOCTYPE_SYNC_MODE=migrate

docs.title: Dependency slimming
docs.text:
The service image is built from pip install frappe + pip install erpnext (Containerfile). Frappe's dependency list assumes a full Desk install — PDF printing, Excel import, 2FA QR codes, full-text search, an interactive console, Google integrations. A headless microservice uses almost none of it.

Two build steps remove what a service cannot reach. Both are measured, not guessed, and both are re-verifiable with scripts/check_pruned_deps.py.

Before After Image size 948 MB 433 MB (−54%) Python distributions 174 126 of which packages 636 MB 254 MB

This library declares 12 dependencies. Everything removed below came from Frappe, not from here.

docs.title: 1. Installing only the dependencies a service needs
docs.text:
Frappe declares ~75 dependencies in pyproject.toml. It ships no requirements.txt, so there is nothing to override — and two entries are git URLs (PyPika, gunicorn) that must survive verbatim.

Rather than install all of them and uninstall the unused ones afterwards — which wastes the download and makes the build log claim we ship packages we do not — the Containerfile installs frappe and erpnext with --no-deps, then asks their installed metadata what they declare and installs that minus an exclusion list:

pip install --no-deps git+.../frappe@${FRAPPE_VERSION}
pip install --no-deps git+.../erpnext@${ERPNEXT_VERSION}
python scripts/resolve_frappe_deps.py > /tmp/frappe-deps.txt
pip install -r /tmp/frappe-deps.txt

Because the list comes from Frappe's own metadata at build time, a version bump picks up new dependencies automatically. Only scripts/excluded_packages.txt is hand-maintained — the part that needs human judgement.

Two supporting files:

File Purpose scripts/excluded_packages.txt The exclusion list. Single source of truth, grouped by capability scripts/extra_packages.txt Packages Frappe/ERPNext import without declaring. Under the old flow these arrived by accident as someone else's transitive dependency; --no-deps makes the gap visible

extra_packages.txt currently holds lxml. ERPNext's EDI modules import it directly but nothing declares it — it used to arrive via premailer, which is excluded. check_pruned_deps.py is what surfaced this. When a package turns out to be needed, add it there; never widen the exclusion list to fix it.

docs.title: How the exclusion list was produced
docs.text:
Boot the service against a live site and dump sys.modules. A real boot loads 205 top-level modules. Anything absent from that set is a candidate:

frappe.init(...); frappe.connect()
# import the library, load a doc, resolve a doctype's meta
tops = {m.split(".")[0] for m in sys.modules}

Notably frappe/app.py — Frappe's own WSGI entry, which top-level imports babel, sentry-sdk and num2words — never loads, because services run Flask.

docs.title: Excluded
docs.text: duckdb (imported nowhere in Frappe at all) · google-api-python-client and its auth stack · the ipython tree · the WeasyPrint tree · GitPython · zxcvbn · ldap3 · pycountry · posthog · vobject · rauth · premailer · Faker · PyQRCode · websockets

docs.title: Deliberately kept (installed)
docs.text:
Package(s) Why Pillow, RestrictedPython, croniter, passlib, pdfkit, pypdf, chardet, pyotp, mysqlclient, PyMySQL Present in the boot trace babel, phonenumbers, num2words, markdown2, sentry-sdk Imported inside functions, so removing them fails at feature-use rather than at boot — a worse failure mode to introduce without exercising those paths. num2words backs money_in_words on invoices psycopg2-binary Containerfile.postgres needs it Whoosh, xlrd, openpyxl, xlsxwriter, et-xmlfile See the warning below

Boot tracing alone is not sufficient. Whoosh and the Excel packages look obviously Desk-only — absent from the boot trace, each imported by a single Frappe module. Removing them broke 40 modules, including core ERPNext controllers (sales_order, stock_entry, work_order) and frappe.desk.query_report. They are imported transitively from places static analysis does not reveal. This is what check_pruned_deps.py exists to catch.

docs.title: 2. Removed translation catalogues
docs.text: frappe/locale is 46 MB of a 73 MB package — 33 .po files plus one .pot. ERPNext ships its own. frappe/public and erpnext/public (browser assets) go too; a headless service serves no UI.

docs.title: Nothing reads them today
docs.text:
The library never sets frappe.local.lang, and lang is never written to site_config.json. Frappe therefore falls back to:

local.lang = local.conf.lang or "en"     # frappe/__init__.py

on every request, and serves English regardless of which .po files are present. Removing them is a no-op, not a trade-off.

docs.title: Currency is not affected
docs.text:
locale/ contains gettext UI strings only — no currency, locale or number formatting data. All three currency concerns read from the database:

Concern Source Conversion (exchange rates) ERPNext Currency Exchange doctype / external API Formatting (symbol, separators, precision) Currency doctype + currency_precision default Amount in words Currency.fraction / fraction_units + the num2words package

money_in_words wraps its output in frappe._(), so the surrounding words would be English — but they already are, per above. The number, symbol, fraction handling and rate are untouched.

docs.title: If server-side translation is needed later
docs.text:
Shipping .po files back is not sufficient on its own. In order:

  1. Set the language per request. In secure_route, where g.tenant_id is set after authentication, also set frappe.local.lang from the user record or the Accept-Language header. It must run after _restore_frappe_local(), which resets frappe.local on every request. Without this, .po files do nothing — which is the situation the removal documents.
  2. Reinstate only the languages actually sold into (~1.4 MB each), not all 33.

The recommended alternative is to translate at the edge: services return a stable error code plus params, and the client — which owns the user's locale and already has an i18n catalogue for its own UI — renders the text. secure_route's error handling (where TenantAccessError and MASK_PERMISSION_ERRORS are handled) is the natural place to map ERPNext exceptions to codes, passing unmapped ones through as an English message exactly as happens today.

docs.title: 3. Removed the git binary from the runtime stage
docs.text:
Worth 104 MB. Only three Frappe call sites use it, all dev/reporting: build.py (asset building) and utils/change_log.py (the About-dialog version lookup). Both shell out to git -C ../apps/<app> — a path that does not exist in this image, so git was already non-functional here. GitPython is pruned for the same reason.

The builder stage still needs it, for pip install git+https://....

docs.title: Two packages that look removable but are not
docs.text: Package Why it stays babel (27.5 MB) Not frontend-only. frappe/utils/data.py uses it in format_date, format_time, format_datetime, global_date_format, pretty_date, comma_or and comma_and — the last builds ERPNext validation messages (Items 'A', 'B' and 'C' ...). Its from babel import Locale sits outside the surrounding try, so an ImportError propagates and a routine validation error becomes a crash markdown2 (<1.6 MB) Most callers are website rendering, printview and website_search, but frappe/email/__init__.py reaches it via frappe.utils.markdown(). Under 1.6 MB is not worth a broken email path

docs.title: Verifying a build
docs.text: Two checks, and they cover different things.

docs.title: 1. Import-level: check_pruned_deps.py
docs.text:
CI runs this before the image is pushed (build job). Run it by hand against any image, and especially after a Frappe upgrade — a new release can add a top-level import and silently invalidate the prune list:

podman run --rm --entrypoint /opt/venv/bin/python \
    <image> /app/scripts/check_pruned_deps.py

It boots the service, then walk-imports every Frappe and ERPNext module, exiting non-zero if anything breaks outside the features intentionally dropped. The allowed-failure list is in the script, with a justification for each entry.

Modules expected to fail, because their whole purpose is a pruned feature: Google integrations, LDAP settings, telemetry, WeasyPrint, password strength, boilerplate, frappe.commands, frappe.gettext, and frappe.patches / frappe.utils.install (migrate-time only — the service image has no bench, and schema sync goes through presync_service_doctypes).

docs.title: 2. Runtime: the integration suite, from inside the image
docs.text:
scripts/run_integration_tests.sh runs tests/integration/ inside the central-site bench container, which has the full unpruned Frappe install. It validates the library, but proves nothing about the image being shipped — a broken prune still shows all green there.

scripts/run_service_image_integration.sh closes that gap. It pairs the built service image with central-site's MariaDB and Redis and runs the same suite from inside the image, exactly as a microservice connects in production:

SERVICE_IMAGE=localhost/frappe-microservice-lib:latest \
    ./scripts/run_service_image_integration.sh

Expected: 12 passed, 9 skipped, 0 failed.

The 9 skips are all of test_tenant_id_stamping.py. Every test in that module asserts on tenancy_app's "*" before_insert hook, which service images deliberately do not ship — the library's get_valid_dict patch is the replacement. Its guard checks both that the app is recorded as installed (frappe.get_installed_apps(), a database read) and that this process can import it. Running a service image against a central-site database is what makes those two diverge; checking only the first was a latent bug, invisible for as long as the suite only ever ran inside central-site.

One suite per stack. Do not run both scripts against the same live containers. Both mutate the shared site database, and each leaves state that breaks the other — verified in both directions. Each script tears down with down -v so every invocation starts clean.

docs.title: Why import-level checking is not enough on its own
docs.text: check_pruned_deps.py catches anything that fails to import. It cannot catch a package that imports fine but is needed at call time — which is precisely the risk class behind keeping babel, phonenumbers, num2words, markdown2 and sentry-sdk. Only running real requests against the image covers those.

docs.title: Package inventories
docs.text:
A stock pip install frappe erpnext produces 174 distributions (636.7 MB). The slimmed service image keeps 126 of them (409.8 MB):

Status Count Size shipped 126 409.8 MB excluded — named in scripts/excluded_packages.txt 39 218.9 MB dropped (transitive) — only required by something excluded 9 8.0 MB

Regenerate the full per-package breakdown from a built image with scripts/resolve_frappe_deps.py, and verify a build against the exclusion list with scripts/check_pruned_deps.py.

docs.title: Packages that look removable but are not
docs.text:
Five distributions carry do not remove: Whoosh, openpyxl, xlsxwriter, xlrd, et-xmlfile. They look Desk-only and never appear in a boot trace, but ERPNext controllers reach them transitively — removing them broke 40 modules including sales_order, stock_entry and work_order. Decide exclusions from a dependency graph, not from a boot trace: a package several kept packages depend on is a very different proposition from a leaf.

Inventory sizes are measured on arm64, so they are internally consistent but larger than what ships. The same build is 948 MB upstream / 433 MB slimmed on arm64, and 371 MB slimmed on linux/amd64, which is what CI reports.

docs.title: What CI checks
docs.text:
Job When What it covers test every push / PR unit suite integration-test every push / PR tests/integration/ inside the central-site bench container — validates the library, but has the full unpruned Frappe install, so it cannot detect a bad exclusion build → Verify nothing broke every push / PR, before the push check_pruned_deps.py against a locally built amd64 image. A broken exclusion list blocks publication verify-image pushes to main, or manual dispatch run_service_image_integration.sh — tests/integration/ from inside the published image against a real database

The import-level gate sits in build because it is cheap: it builds amd64 only and loads it locally, so the multi-arch push that follows reuses the buildx cache and only arm64 is new work.

verify-image is deliberately not run per-PR. It pulls the central-site image (several GB), which integration-test already pulls on its own runner, and the gate in build already stops a broken image from being published. It pulls the image build just pushed rather than rebuilding it.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The image is built for linux/amd64 only.

GitHub-hosted ARM runners (ubuntu-24.04-arm) are free for public repositories only. This repo is private on a free plan, so an arm64 job would never be assigned a runner. The alternative — emulating arm64 through QEMU — cost about 14.6 minutes per build for an architecture nothing currently deploys on, so it was removed along with the QEMU setup step.

To add arm64 later, follow the pattern in a sibling project's container-build.yml: a native runner per architecture pushing :tag-amd64 and :tag-arm64, then docker buildx imagetools create to stitch the manifest, plus a check that the published manifest really lists both. That needs a paid plan, a public repo, or self-hosted ARM runners.

Note that image sizes differ by architecture: the same build measures 433 MB on an arm64 host and 371 MB on linux/amd64, which is what CI reports and what gets deployed.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/vyogotech/erpnext-microservices-lib.git
cd erpnext-microservices-lib
pip install -e ".[dev]"
make setup          # installs and registers the pre-commit hooks

make setup and make lint are the only Make targets.

docs.title: Python versions
docs.text:
There is no single version — each context pins its own, which matters when reproducing a failure:

Context Python CI test job 3.10 Containerfile, Containerfile.dev 3.14 Containerfile.postgres 3.11 .devcontainer 3.11

The package requires 3.10+ (setup.py), because it uses PEP 604 unions without from __future__ import annotations.

docs.title: Dev container
docs.text:
.devcontainer/ is configured for VS Code — open the project and choose "Reopen in Container".

The dev container is currently stale

.devcontainer/Dockerfile installs Frappe and ERPNext from version-15, but the library imports frappe.utils.local, which only exists in v16. Code touching MicroserviceApp will fail to import there. Its compose file also defines a single service — no MariaDB, no Redis — so nothing needing a live site runs in it.

Use the integration scripts below for anything requiring a real site.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Three suites, run differently.

docs.title: Unit tests
docs.text:
pytest -m "not integration" tests/

The -m "not integration" filter matters — without it pytest collects the integration suite, which needs a live Frappe site. pytest.ini applies branch coverage with an 80% --cov-fail-under gate and writes HTML to htmlcov/.

./run_tests.sh [unit|integration|all] wraps the same commands.

docs.title: BDD tests
docs.text: behave features/

docs.title: Integration tests
docs.text:
These run inside a container with a real Frappe site, MariaDB and Redis. Two harnesses, answering two different questions:

# Does the library work against a real site?
./scripts/run_integration_tests.sh

# Does the SHIPPED SERVICE IMAGE work? (pruned dependencies and all)
SERVICE_IMAGE=localhost/frappe-microservice-lib:latest \
  ./scripts/run_service_image_integration.sh

Both start the public docker.io/vyogo/erpnext:sne-version-16 image with MULTI_TENANT=0, bind-mount the repo at /mnt/lib, and tear down on exit. KEEP_RUNNING=1 leaves the containers up for debugging; override the image with CENTRAL_SITE_IMAGE.

One suite per stack

Do not run both scripts against the same live containers. Both mutate the shared site database and each breaks the other — verified in both directions. KEEP_RUNNING=1 defeats the clean-start guarantee, so start fresh when switching.

The integration suite has no coverage gate — tests/integration/pytest.ini sets only the marker and a 120s timeout.

docs.title: Linting
docs.text:
Local and CI lint with different tools. CI runs flake8 frappe_microservice/ against setup.cfg (max line length 120, with cosmetic codes ignored so the baseline still catches real pyflakes errors). Pre-commit runs a different stack:

make lint          # pre-commit run --all-files
Hook What it does ruff + ruff-format Lint and format lizard Complexity ≤ 15 per function, ≤ 450 lines per file semgrep Static security analysis (--config=auto) gitleaks Secret scanning whitespace hooks Trailing whitespace, EOF newline, large files

Two things to know before trusting a green or red run:

  • ruff runs without --fix, deliberately. Autofix once removed a live import and produced a NameError; the hook reports rather than rewrites.
  • Some hooks fail on pre-existing code. Establish the baseline on an untouched checkout before assuming a failure is yours.

Because CI enforces only flake8, run that directly before pushing:

flake8 frappe_microservice/

docs.title: Where to make changes
docs.text:
If you are changing… Edit MicroserviceApp, middleware, secure_route, logging, OTEL app.py OAuth2 / SID / internal-token validation auth.py Embedded RQ worker, enqueue_task background.py Redis key namespacing for a shared cache cache.py CentralSiteClient (app.central) central.py The frappe-ms CLI cli.py DocType controller system controller.py Container startup order, Gunicorn exec entrypoint.py DocumentHooks lifecycle system hooks.py App/module isolation, hook filtering isolation.py Tenant-scoped docnames, resolve_or_create naming.py off/warn/enforce and boolean flag parsing policy.py Link-value label presentation presentation.py Startup DocType schema and fixture sync presync.py register_resource() auto-CRUD resources.py site_config.json generation site_config.py TenantAwareDB, tenant resolution and stamping tenant.py Public API re-exports __init__.py (and core.py for compatibility)

Patch targets in tests

unittest.mock.patch() must target the module where a symbol is used at runtime, not where it is re-exported. Patch frappe_microservice.app.get_user_tenant_id — where MicroserviceApp imports it — not frappe_microservice.core.get_user_tenant_id. tests/test_patch_target_guard.py enforces this.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Do not break public API signatures. Add keyword arguments with defaults; never reorder or remove parameters.
  • New enforcement ships as warn first. Add the flag, default it to log-only, document the 2.0 default, and give operators a release to discover what would break. See Security.
  • Keep the coverage gate. 80% with branch coverage; do not lower it to make a change fit.
  • Update the CHANGELOG under [Unreleased], and the docs alongside the code.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
Allure is wired into both suites:

pytest -m "not integration" --alluredir=allure-results tests/
behave -f allure_behave.formatter:AllureFormatter -o allure-results features/
allure serve allure-results

docs.title: Auto-CRUD resources
docs.text:
register_resource() exposes a DocType as a REST resource — authenticated, tenant-scoped and documented in Swagger, with no handler code:

app = create_microservice("orders-service")
app.register_resource("Sales Order")

GET    /api/resource/sales-order         list
POST   /api/resource/sales-order         create
GET    /api/resource/sales-order/{name}  read
PUT    /api/resource/sales-order/{name}  update
DELETE /api/resource/sales-order/{name}  delete

List routes accept the usual Frappe query parameters (filters, fields, limit, order_by).

docs.title: Secure endpoints
docs.text:
secure_route authenticates the caller against the Central Site and injects the resolved user:

@app.secure_route("/orders/summary", methods=["GET"])
def order_summary(user):
    orders = app.tenant_db.get_all("Sales Order", filters={"status": "Draft"})
    return {"user": user, "count": len(orders)}

Use app.route(...) for a deliberately public endpoint — it takes no user.

docs.title: Document controllers
docs.text:
Organise business logic in Frappe-style classes:

# controllers/sales_order.py
from frappe_microservice.controller import DocumentController

class SalesOrder(DocumentController):
    def validate(self):
        if not self.customer:
            self.throw("Customer is required")

    def before_insert(self):
        self.status = self.status or "Draft"

Register them once:

from frappe_microservice import setup_controllers
setup_controllers(app, controllers_directory="./controllers")

Controllers are auto-discovered from $SERVICE_PATH/controllers/ when that directory exists, and run during insert and update — including from background jobs.

docs.title: Document hooks
docs.text:
For logic that does not warrant a class, or that spans DocTypes:

@app.tenant_db.on("Sales Order", "before_insert")
def set_defaults(doc):
    doc.status = doc.status or "Draft"

@app.tenant_db.on("*", "after_insert")     # every DocType
def audit(doc):
    app.logger.info("created %s %s", doc.doctype, doc.name)

Events: before_validate, validate, before_insert, after_insert, before_update, after_update, before_delete, after_delete.

docs.title: Background tasks
docs.text:
An embedded RQ worker runs as a daemon thread inside the service container — no separate worker deployment. It is off by default; enable with ENABLE_RQ=1.

@app.secure_route("/reports", methods=["POST"])
def trigger_report(user):
    app.enqueue_task(build_report, user, period="monthly")
    return {"status": "enqueued"}

def build_report(user, period=None):
    import frappe
    # full Frappe API available — context is restored for you
    frappe.get_doc({...}).insert()
    frappe.db.commit()

The worker restores frappe.local and the database connection, so jobs behave like request handlers. Controller discovery works there too.

Calling enqueue_task() with ENABLE_RQ unset raises RuntimeError rather than silently dropping the job.

Job timeouts need a forking worker

RQ_DEFAULT_JOB_TIMEOUT sets a default, but the embedded worker is a SimpleWorker and cannot enforce it. For hard timeouts, set WORKER_MODE=1 (which starts the queue without the thread) and run frappe-ms worker as a separate forking process.

RQ connects via REDIS_URL, which is separate from the REDIS_HOST / REDIS_PORT pair that feeds site_config.json. Setting one does not configure the other.

Background jobs run outside a request, so there is no session and no tenant context. In multi-tenant mode, pass the tenant explicitly to anything a job writes.

docs.title: Central Site client
docs.text:
app.central calls back to the Central Site with a Frappe-like API. It is lazily initialised — no connection is attempted until first use.

@app.secure_route("/sync", methods=["POST"])
def sync(user):
    tenant = app.central.get_doc("Tenant", "tenant-123")
    app.central.update("Tenant", "tenant-123", {"status": "Active"})
    result = app.central.call("some_whitelisted_method", {"param": "value"})
    return {"status": "synced"}

Authenticate with either an API key/secret pair or a username/password — see Configuration.

docs.title: Swagger / OpenAPI
docs.text:
Every service exposes interactive docs at /apidocs, and the raw spec at /apispec_1.json. Registered resources are documented automatically.

Document custom endpoints with YAML in the docstring:

@app.secure_route("/orders/summary", methods=["GET"])
def order_summary(user):
    """
    Get an order summary for the current tenant
    ---
    tags: [Orders]
    parameters:
      - name: days
        in: query
        type: integer
        default: 7
    responses:
      200:
        description: Summary retrieved
    """
    return {"total_orders": 100}

docs.title: Health & readiness probes
docs.text:
Two endpoints, because liveness and readiness answer different questions:

  • GET /health — liveness. Never queries the database; reports the connection state as connected or pending. Restarting a container because the database is briefly unreachable makes an outage worse, so this stays cheap.
  • GET /health/ready — readiness. Runs SELECT 1; returns 200, or 503 with {"status": "not_ready"} when the database is unreachable. Point your orchestrator's readiness probe here so traffic stops without a restart loop.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text: All framework errors share one JSON shape, and Frappe exceptions map to sensible HTTP status codes. Tracebacks appear only under DEBUG=1 — see Security.

docs.title: Tenant-aware database
docs.text: app.tenant_db wraps the Frappe ORM with tenant scoping, permission checks and lifecycle hooks. Its behaviour depends on the tenancy mode — see Tenancy.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Central Site — a running Frappe site acting as the authentication provider. Services validate every request against it.
  • A tenancy provider app — only for multi-tenant deployments. Single-tenant mode runs against a stock site; see Tenancy.

The library requires Frappe v16. It imports frappe.utils.local, which does not exist in v15.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install frappe-microservice

From source:

git clone https://github.com/vyogotech/erpnext-microservices-lib.git
cd erpnext-microservices-lib
pip install -e .

docs.title: Your first service
docs.text:
A server.py with one authenticated endpoint:

from frappe_microservice import create_microservice

app = create_microservice("my-service")

@app.secure_route("/hello", methods=["GET"])
def hello(user):
    # `user` is injected once the session is validated against the Central Site
    return {"message": f"Hello {user}!"}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()

Point it at a Central Site and a database, then run it:

export CENTRAL_SITE_URL=http://central-site:8000
export FRAPPE_SITE=dev.localhost
export DB_HOST=localhost
export MULTI_TENANT=0        # stock site, no tenancy provider

python server.py

Interactive API docs are at http://localhost:8000/apidocs.

docs.title: Exposing a DocType
docs.text:
The shortest path from a DocType to a REST API:

app = create_microservice("orders-service")
app.register_resource("Sales Order")
app.run()

That registers list, create, read, update and delete routes under /api/resource/sales-order, all authenticated, tenant-scoped and documented in Swagger. See Core Features.

docs.title: Choosing a tenancy mode
docs.text:
MULTI_TENANT=1 (default) MULTI_TENANT=0 Site Needs a Central Site tenancy provider Stock Frappe/ERPNext Reads Scoped by tenant_id Unscoped Writes Stamped with tenant_id Not stamped Role permissions Enforced Enforced

Start with MULTI_TENANT=0 if you are evaluating the library or serving a single organisation — it needs nothing beyond a stock site. Tenancy covers the Central Site contract multi-tenant mode expects.

An empty value is not off

MULTI_TENANT="" resolves to the default (on), so a missing ConfigMap key cannot silently drop tenant isolation. Disabling requires MULTI_TENANT=0.

docs.title: Running in a container
docs.text:
The base image ships the entrypoint, so a service needs no entrypoint.py — only a server.py that creates the app:

FROM ghcr.io/vyogotech/erpnext-microservices-lib:latest
WORKDIR /app
COPY . /app/service/
RUN touch /app/service/__init__.py
# expose as a Frappe app so the framework can load it ("my-service" -> my_service)
RUN ln -sf /app/service /app/sites/apps/my_service
ENV SERVICE_PATH=/app/service
ENV SERVICE_APP=server:app
EXPOSE 8000
Variable Purpose Default SERVICE_PATH Directory holding your service code /app/service SERVICE_APP WSGI target as module:attr server:app

The entrypoint (python -m frappe_microservice.entrypoint) writes site_config.json from the environment, runs the DocType sync once, and then execs Gunicorn. Use SERVICE_APP=main:app for a different module or attribute.

Use immutable image tags in production — every build publishes sha-<full>. latest only ever tracks main. See CI/CD.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Configuration — every environment variable and kwarg
  • Core Features — controllers, hooks, background jobs, Swagger
  • Tenancy — modes and the Central Site contract
  • Security — policy modes, authentication, SQL safety
  • Architecture — bounded context and isolation

docs.title: Tracing (OpenTelemetry)
docs.text:
Tracing is off until you point it at a collector:

export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT="http://jaeger:4317"

With it unset the framework logs tracing disabled and adds no overhead. If the OpenTelemetry packages are not installed, tracing is a no-op rather than an error.

The OTel service.name comes from the app's name — create_microservice("orders-service") reports as orders-service. There is no environment variable for it.

docs.title: What is instrumented
docs.text:
• HTTP requests — every incoming request, via Flask instrumentation.
  • Database operations — TenantAwareDB.get_all, get_doc and insert_doc emit manual spans carrying db.system, db.operation, db.target (the DocType) and, where known, the document name.

Spans are exported through a BatchSpanProcessor, so a slow or unreachable collector does not block request handling. It will, however, log export failures — if you see repeated Failed to export traces warnings, the endpoint is wrong or the collector is down.

The OpenTelemetry packages ship in the base install for 1.5.0 and are also available as the [otel] extra. They move to extra-only in 2.0.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
LOG_LEVEL sets the level (default INFO); an unrecognised name silently falls back to INFO.

export LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG

docs.title: Container-safe logging
docs.text:
Frappe's default handlers write to files whose paths resolve relative to the process working directory — a bench-era assumption. Under a container WORKDIR, or a read-only root filesystem, that crashes with FileNotFoundError: .../logs/database.log.

The library therefore sets FRAPPE_STREAM_LOGGING=1 at import: logs go to stderr, which is what Kubernetes and Docker collect, and no *.log file is ever opened. This is the 12-factor behaviour and the reason services boot cleanly on a read-only filesystem.

To opt back into bench-style file logs, set FRAPPE_STREAM_LOGGING="" before importing the library.

Read-only root filesystems

Even with stream logging, the sites directory must stay writable — site_config.json is written there at startup. Mount an emptyDir over it when running with readOnlyRootFilesystem: true.

docs.title: Health probes
docs.text: Point your orchestrator at the right endpoint for the right question — /health for liveness, /health/ready for readiness. Using the readiness endpoint as a liveness probe turns a brief database outage into a restart loop. See Core Features.

docs.title: Policy modes
docs.text:
Several protections ship in warn-only mode: they log what would be blocked but block nothing. This lets you deploy the upgrade, read the logs, fix what surfaces, and then enforce — instead of discovering breakage in production.

They flip to enforce by default in 2.0. Set them explicitly in production rather than relying on either default.

Env var Kwarg Values Current default 2.0 default Purpose PERMISSION_MODE permission_mode off\|warn\|enforce warn enforce Role-permission checks on tenant_db reads and set_value CSRF_MODE csrf_mode off\|warn\|enforce warn enforce CSRF signal required for cookie-authenticated mutations TENANT_STRICT tenant_strict off\|warn\|enforce warn enforce Fail closed when a table lacks a tenant_id column MASK_PERMISSION_ERRORS mask_permission_errors 1/true/… off on Mask cross-tenant probes as 404 (anti-enumeration)

An unrecognised value logs a warning and falls back to the default rather than failing to boot.

TENANT_STRICT has no effect while MULTI_TENANT=0 — see Tenancy.

docs.title: Finding what enforcement would break
docs.text:
In warn mode every would-be denial is logged with a [would-deny] prefix:

[would-deny] permission read on Sales Invoice for user alice@example.com (mode=warn)

Grep for [would-deny] in a representative window of traffic. An empty result means enforce is safe to turn on.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Three mechanisms, all validated against the Central Site.

docs.title: OAuth2 Bearer tokens
docs.text:
For API clients and service-to-service calls:

curl -X POST http://central-site:8000/oauth/token \
  -d grant_type=client_credentials \
  -d client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID \
  -d client_secret=YOUR_SECRET

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  http://localhost:8000/api/resource/sales-order

docs.title: Session cookies (SID)
docs.text:
For browser clients using a normal Frappe login:

await fetch("http://central-site:8000/api/method/login", {
  method: "POST",
  credentials: "include",
  body: JSON.stringify({ usr: "user@example.com", pwd: "password" }),
});

// the sid cookie is sent automatically
await fetch("http://localhost:8000/api/resource/sales-order", {
  credentials: "include",
});

docs.title: Internal service token
docs.text:
For trusted service-to-service traffic that should not carry a user session, set INTERNAL_SERVICE_TOKEN and send it as X-Internal-Token. A valid token is granted the identity in INTERNAL_SERVICE_USER (default Administrator).

Prefer a scoped service user

INTERNAL_SERVICE_USER is not validated against the database at authentication time — the connection may not be up yet — so a nonexistent user fails later, at the first permission check. Use a dedicated service user with only the roles it needs rather than Administrator, which is platform-level and cannot own tenant data.

docs.title: Which methods are CSRF-exempt
docs.text:
CSRF_MODE only affects the sid cookie path, because browsers attach cookies automatically. These are immune and never checked:

  • Authorization: Bearer
  • X-Internal-Token
  • the X-Frappe-SID header
  • GET, HEAD, OPTIONS

The accepted signal is an X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest header. A full Frappe CSRF-token round-trip is a planned follow-up.

docs.title: Prefer the TenantAwareDB helpers
docs.text:
# Good — tenant filtering and permission checks are applied for you
orders = app.tenant_db.get_all("Sales Order", filters={"status": "Draft"})

# Bad — raw SQL bypasses both; you own the tenant filter
orders = frappe.db.sql("SELECT * FROM `tabSales Order` WHERE status='Draft'")

Raw SQL bypasses role-permission checks by design. Under PERMISSION_MODE=enforce each such call is logged so audits can find them.

docs.title: Always parameterise
docs.text:
When raw SQL is unavoidable, pass parameters — never interpolate:

# Good
tenant_id = app.tenant_db.get_tenant_id()
orders = app.tenant_db.sql(
    "SELECT * FROM `tabSales Order` WHERE tenant_id = %s AND status = %s",
    (tenant_id, "Draft"),
    as_dict=True,
)

# NEVER — f-strings and % formatting are injection vectors
orders = app.tenant_db.sql(
    f"SELECT * FROM `tabSales Order` WHERE tenant_id = '{tenant_id}'"
)

This applies to the tenant id as much as to user input.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
ALLOW_CORS is written into site_config.json as allow_cors. Left unset it defaults to * and logs a warning — acceptable for local development, not for production. Set an explicit origin:

ALLOW_CORS=https://app.example.com

docs.title: Error responses
docs.text:
Framework errors use one JSON shape:

{
  "status": "error",
  "message": "Human readable message",
  "type": "ExceptionClass",
  "code": 403
}

Frappe exceptions map to HTTP status codes: PermissionError → 403, DoesNotExistError → 404, ValidationError → 400, authentication failures → 401.

Exception strings and tracebacks appear in 500 bodies only when DEBUG=1 (or Flask debug is on). Otherwise error and details are null, so internal detail is not leaked to callers.

docs.title: Secret scanning
docs.text: gitleaks runs as a pre-commit hook alongside semgrep for static analysis. See Development for the hook setup.

docs.title: Tenancy
docs.text:
The framework runs in one of two modes, selected by MULTI_TENANT. Both are first-class; neither is a degraded version of the other.

MULTI_TENANT=1 (default) MULTI_TENANT=0 Site Needs a Central Site tenancy provider Stock Frappe/ERPNext Reads Scoped by tenant_id Unscoped Writes Stamped with tenant_id Not stamped get_doc Verifies tenant ownership No tenant check Master docnames Tenant-scoped (<tenant8>-<slug>) Frappe autonaming Startup DDL Adds a tenant_id column per DocType None Role permissions Enforced Enforced — unchanged

An empty value is not off

MULTI_TENANT="" resolves to the default (on), not to off. A declared but valueless environment variable — a Kubernetes env: entry with no value, or a missing ConfigMap key — must not silently drop tenant isolation. Disabling requires an explicit MULTI_TENANT=0.

docs.title: Multi-tenant mode
docs.text:
A single site holds every tenant's rows, separated by a tenant_id column. app.tenant_db applies that separation automatically, so handler code does not carry tenant logic:

# scoped to the caller's tenant — no filter written by hand
orders = app.tenant_db.get_all("Sales Order", filters={"status": "Draft"})

# stamped with the caller's tenant
app.tenant_db.insert_doc("Sales Order", {"customer": "CUST-001"})

# raises TenantAccessError if the document belongs to another tenant
order = app.tenant_db.get_doc("Sales Order", "SO-0001")

docs.title: The Central Site contract
docs.text:
Multi-tenant mode expects the Central Site to run an app providing tenancy. The framework depends on no particular implementation — only on this contract:

  1. Tenant identity — a tenant_id field on the User DocType.
  2. Column presence — a tenant_id column on the tables services read and write. Frappe keeps tenant_id outside DocType metadata, so a provider normally adds it with an ALTER TABLE patch across every non-single DocType.
  3. Session response — session validation returns the user's tenant_id, so a service can resolve the tenant from a session alone.

Any app meeting that contract works. Without one, multi-tenant mode cannot function: the service cannot resolve a tenant, and tenant-scoped writes fail because the column is absent.

docs.title: Why writes need the column on every table
docs.text:
The stamping patch assumes every non-single table carries tenant_id. Measured on an ERPNext site with a provider's patch applied, 753 of 756 tables do. The three that do not — tabSeries, tabSessions, tabSingles — are framework stores written by raw SQL or update_single, never through a DocType insert.

That is why a site without the patch fails loudly rather than degrading: the first child-row insert raises OperationalError 1054 instead of silently writing rows under a default tenant that no tenant can read back.

docs.title: Tenant-scoped docnames
docs.text:
Field-autonamed master doctypes (Item, Customer, Supplier, …) would collide when two tenants create "Acme Corp". The framework prefixes their docnames with the first 8 characters of the tenant id, matching what a Central Site tenancy hook produces so both converge on the same primary key.

Two tenant ids sharing their first 8 hex characters collapse to the same prefix. That is cosmetic, not an isolation hole — collisions get a numeric suffix and lookups stay tenant-filtered.

docs.title: Single-tenant mode
docs.text:
Set MULTI_TENANT=0 and the framework resolves, filters on, stamps and verifies no tenant_id at all. It runs against a stock Frappe/ERPNext site with no tenancy provider and no tenant_id column anywhere.

Use it when:

  • one deployment serves one organisation;
  • you want to adopt the framework before committing to a tenancy provider;
  • you are running the integration suite (which is exactly what CI does).

What changes internally, beyond the query paths:

  • secure_route skips the per-request tenant lookup. On a stock site that lookup would query a tenant_id column on tabUser that does not exist — two failing queries and three error log lines on every authenticated request.
  • presync does not add tenant_id columns. This one matters: re-creating the column would quietly reintroduce the dependency this mode exists to remove.
  • Master docnames fall back to Frappe autonaming.
  • Link presentation is inert, because nothing was renamed to present.

docs.title: What does not change
docs.text:
Role permissions still apply. PERMISSION_MODE is orthogonal to tenancy — a single-tenant site still has Roles, DocPerms, and users who should not read Purchase Invoices. Single-tenant mode is not "no checks".

TENANT_STRICT is deliberately ignored while the mode is off. Its purpose is to flag tables missing a tenant_id column, which on a stock site is every table: the default warn would log on every read, and enforce would make the mode impossible.

docs.title: Choosing at runtime
docs.text:
Both forms are equivalent; the environment variable is the usual choice for containers:

app = create_microservice("my-service", multi_tenant=False)

MULTI_TENANT=0

The keyword argument wins over the environment variable, which wins over the default. See Configuration for the resolution rules.
